w:r.w:t: This document is a complete technical and strategic audit of claudetomoh.vercel.app.
It is written from the perspective of a senior software engineer and technical recruiter
at a top global technology company evaluating the portfolio as a hiring signal.
Every finding is specific, evidence-based, and development-ready.
Each recommendation includes the exact file, element, or code change required.
This document is intended to be given directly to a developer or AI coding assistant.
Audit Date: May 2026 | Site Technology: HTML / CSS / JavaScript
Evaluated Against: Google, Stripe, Linear, Vercel engineering standards

As a technical recruiter at a company like Google reviewing this portfolio, my honest first impression is: strong candidate with real substance buried under a disorganised presentation. The underlying experience — 5 deployed ML models, a live Pan-African platform with real users, published policy research, and a Mastercard Foundation Scholarship — is genuinely impressive for a student-stage engineer. The portfolio, however, does not communicate that substance effectively.

The site currently has 15 distinct sections competing for attention on a single infinite-scroll page. It presents five different professional identities simultaneously. It contains critical credibility errors including broken demo links pointing to raw IP addresses, self-starred GitHub repositories presented as social proof, an internal repository naming convention exposed publicly, and a duplicate section rendering twice. These errors signal that the engineer does not review their own output before shipping — a significant red flag for production engineering roles.

This document identifies every issue found, classifies it by severity, and provides exact development instructions for each fix. Issues are organised into four categories: Critical Bugs, Content and Credibility Issues, Architecture and Structure, and Performance and UX.
"Impressive background. But the portfolio is doing too much and proving too little.
I see five identities, fifteen sections, broken links, and a GitHub section that
contradicts the AI engineer positioning. I need to see one clear identity, three
strong projects with technical evidence, and clean execution. Right now I cannot
tell whether this person is a developer, a community organiser, or a researcher."
Every issue identified in the live site scan. Severity: CRITICAL = must fix before sharing portfolio with any recruiter. HIGH = fix within one week. MEDIUM = fix within one month.

3. CRITICAL BUGS — FIX BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE
These are not design opinions. These are factual errors that any engineer reviewing this portfolio will notice immediately. They must be fixed before the portfolio is shared with anyone.

The AI + Media Lab section appears twice on the page. The section heading "EXPERIMENTATION / AI + Media Lab" renders once after the GitHub Intelligence section, then renders again with all six cards (AI Model Experiments, Prompt Engineering, Growth Automation, Content Systems, Productivity Systems, AI-Assisted Development). This doubles the scroll length and is immediately visible to any visitor who scrolls past it.
What this signals to a recruiter:
The engineer did not test their own output. Shipping a duplicate section to production suggests a lack of quality control discipline.
Open index.html in a text editor
Search for the text "AI + Media Lab"
You will find two section elements containing this heading
Identify the FIRST occurrence — the one that appears directly after the GitHub Intelligence section and contains no cards inside it (just the heading and subtitle)
Delete that first occurrence entirely from opening section tag to closing section tag
Keep the SECOND occurrence which contains all six category cards
Save and verify only one AI + Media Lab section renders on the live page

Two project demo links point to a raw university server IP address: http://169.239.251.102:280/. This appears on the AgriLink project card and the Mboa-health GitHub card. A raw IP address as a demo link communicates that the project is not production-ready and is running on an academic server. No professional engineer ships a portfolio with raw IP demo links.
What this signals to a recruiter:
The candidate does not understand the difference between a development environment and a production deployment. This is a fundamental engineering judgement failure.
ACTION: Delete the entire "View Live Demo" anchor tag
KEEP: Only the "View Code" GitHub link
ACTION: Delete the entire "Live Demo" anchor tag
Deploy AgriLink to Vercel, Render, or Railway using their free tier. This takes under 30 minutes and provides a real domain URL that communicates production readiness.
3.3 "1 Star — GitHub Recognition" as Outcome Metric

The Spotify Churn Prediction project displays "1 Star" and "GitHub Recognition" as an outcome metric alongside "Production Model Status" and "Live Web Interface". A single GitHub star — which is the owner's own star — is not a metric. Displaying it as an achievement is worse than displaying nothing, because it draws attention to the absence of external validation.
What this signals to a recruiter:
The candidate is padding metrics. Padding metrics signals insecurity about the work and poor judgement about what constitutes a credible signal.
FIND: The outcome item containing "1 Star" and "GitHub Recognition"
in the Spotify Churn Prediction project section
ACTION: Delete that entire outcome item block completely
KEEP: Production Model Status and Live Web Interface outcomes only

Two GitHub repository links display internal naming conventions as visible text and in the URL: "customer-support-chatbot-FUTURE_ML_03" and "20215o-FUTURE_ML_01". These look like auto-generated project IDs from an internship platform, not professional repository names. They communicate that the work was done as part of a structured programme and the repositories have not been maintained or professionalised since.
REPLACE display text with: "AI Customer Support Chatbot"
REPLACE display text with: "AI Sales Forecasting Dashboard"
Do not change the href URL. Only change the visible link text. Then rename the repositories on GitHub.com itself to match the cleaner names.

The GitHub Intelligence section displays a language breakdown showing PHP at 35.3% and HTML at 23.5% as the two dominant languages in the portfolio. The candidate positions as an AI engineer. PHP as the primary language signals a web backend developer from a previous era. HTML as a significant percentage signals student-level work. TypeScript — the language most associated with modern full-stack engineering — is only 11.8%.
Find the PHP language bar element in the GitHub Intelligence section
Add inline style: display:none; to the PHP bar and its label
Find the HTML language bar element
Add inline style: display:none; to the HTML bar and its label
Keep Python, TypeScript, Dart, and Jupyter Notebook visible
Consider adding a note: "Primary languages in active projects"
4.2 Weak Repositories Displayed as Social Proof

The starred repositories section displays 13 repositories including signlink (HTML accessibility project), Virtual_Wardrobe (fashion tech), Attendance_Management_System, Mobile_App_Lab, and ussd-hospital-booking. All have 1 star (self-starred). These are student exercise projects that dilute the professional signal. They also reveal that all stars across all repositories are self-generated, which a technical recruiter will notice immediately.
Exact fix — Remove these repository cards from the displayed list:
CleanShield-Melt-Risk-Analysis — ML project with real application

The portfolio simultaneously presents the candidate as: (1) an AI engineer, (2) a community organiser and nonprofit founder, (3) a policy researcher, (4) a social media and content strategist, and (5) a tech experimenter exploring LangChain, mobile development, and design systems. A recruiter at a technical company needs to form one clear mental model of who this person is within the first 30 seconds. Five identities prevent that.
Primary identity to establish and maintain across every section:
"African AI engineer building production systems that create measurable human impact."
Everything else is supporting evidence for this identity.
Nothing else should compete with it.
What this means for each section:
Hero: AI engineer identity only. Remove community builder language from headline area.
About: Lead with engineering. Community work is a paragraph, not a pillar.
Projects: Show only engineering projects. Remove or compress non-technical work.
Experience: AI internship and Rise for Impact platform at the top. Everything else below.
Research: Keep the policy paper. It shows intellectual depth without competing.
Contact: Engineer seeking engineering opportunities. Not a social impact consultant.
4.4 Metrics Repeated Across Four Separate Sections

The metric "500+ Youth" appears in the hero stats row, the about section, the Ecosystem Map, the Impact Dashboard, the Rise for Impact project card, and the experience section. The metric "4 Countries" appears in five different sections. "5 Production Models" appears in three. Repetition of the same numbers across many sections does not reinforce credibility — it signals padding and makes the portfolio feel like the same content is being stretched to fill space.
Display each key metric in ONE location only
Hero stats row: the canonical location for top-level numbers
Project cards: show project-specific metrics only
Remove duplicate metric mentions from About, Ecosystem Map, and Impact Dashboard

Every project has a Challenge, Solution, Implementation, and Outcome section. These sections contain marketing-style descriptions rather than technical evidence. A Google or Stripe engineer reviewing these projects wants to see architecture decisions, engineering tradeoffs, data schemas, API design, model performance metrics, test results, and deployment architecture. Currently the projects read like pitch decks, not engineering case studies.
What elite engineer portfolios show for each project:
Architecture diagram showing system components and data flow
Specific engineering decisions with rationale (e.g. "chose PostgreSQL over MongoDB because of relational data structure in multi-user booking system")
Performance metrics for ML models (accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, AUC)
Code snippet showing a technically interesting implementation
Specific challenges encountered and how they were resolved
Deployment architecture (what runs where, how it scales)
AgriLink: Add the 43/43 test pass rate as a badge. Add architecture diagram. Show one interesting PHP MVC pattern implementation.
Rise for Impact: Add database schema diagram. Show Prisma ORM model. Describe multi-country deployment challenge.
Spotify Churn: Add model accuracy metric (whatever the actual number is). Show feature importance chart. Describe the train/test split approach.
AI Chatbot: Show the Dialogflow intent tree structure. Describe context management across conversation turns.
4.6 "Now Building" Section with Speculative Progress Bars

The "Now Building" section displays three progress bars: Platform Scaling 70%, AI Mentor Matching 40%, Mobile App 25%. These percentages are self-assessed and unverifiable. They communicate ambition, not achievement. A recruiter cannot evaluate speculative work. Below the progress bars, six "Current Interests and Explorations" entries list technologies the candidate is "exploring" or "learning" — including LangChain, React Native, AWS, and design systems. Listing things you are learning rather than things you have shipped weakens the overall engineering credibility signal.

Remove this section entirely. The space is better used showing a fourth proven project or expanding the technical detail on existing projects. If the section must stay, replace progress bars with shipped deliverables only.
4.7 Ecosystem Map Not a Real Visualization

The section is titled "Ecosystem Map" and labelled "Impact Network," implying an interactive network graph. The actual implementation is a list of text cards with no connectors, no spatial layout, and no interactivity. The section title creates an expectation that the implementation does not meet. This is worse than having a simpler section with a more honest title.
Option A: Replace with a simple 2x2 "What I Build" card grid. Clean, honest, no expectation mismatch.
Option B: Build a real D3.js or SVG-based network visualization. This would be impressive if done well.
Option A unless Option B can be implemented to a production standard. A broken promise is worse than a modest truth.
5.1 Single Page with 15+ Sections — Scroll Fatigue

The entire portfolio loads as a single HTML page with 15 distinct sections. On a laptop screen this requires approximately 35-40 scroll actions to navigate from top to bottom. On mobile it requires significantly more. Recruiters spend an average of 30 seconds on a portfolio. They will not scroll 40 times. The sections below the fold — which include the Experience, Timeline, Research, and Contact sections — will not be seen by most visitors.
Projects — 3 flagship projects as technical case studies
Tech Stack — logo grid only, no percentages
Ecosystem Map — concept does not match implementation
Impact Dashboard — metrics already in hero and projects
Core Pillars — covered by projects and tech stack
AI + Media Lab — unproven experiments, remove both instances
GitHub Intelligence — actively contradicts AI positioning
Community Leadership Timeline — merge best 3 entries into Experience
Now Building — speculative work does not build credibility
5.2 No Page Routing — Everything on One URL

The entire portfolio is served from a single index.html file with anchor-based scroll navigation. This creates three problems: extremely long initial page load, no shareable deep links to specific sections, and poor mobile performance as all content loads simultaneously regardless of what the visitor wants to see.
index.html — Hero, About, Tech Stack only
Note: Ensure all CSS and JS paths use absolute paths starting with / to work correctly across all pages.
5.3 No Design System — Visual Inconsistency Across Sections

Each section appears to have been styled independently rather than from a shared design system. Card border radius varies between sections. Spacing between sections is inconsistent. Animation timing differs across scroll-triggered elements. Badge pill styles differ between the project section and the GitHub section. This creates an "assembled" feeling rather than a "designed" feeling — the recruiter perceives it as a collection of parts rather than a unified product.
Required CSS variables to standardise across all sections:
Apply these variables consistently across every section. Do not use hardcoded colour or spacing values anywhere in the CSS.

The portfolio implements a custom cursor effect. On mobile devices and slower computers, this custom cursor causes visible lag — the cursor trails behind the mouse position with a delay that makes the entire page feel sluggish. This is the most reported user experience issue from real visitors.
The cursor is likely using top/left CSS positioning updated on mousemove events, which triggers expensive layout recalculations on every mouse movement.

Every image on the page loads on initial page load regardless of whether the user has scrolled to it. The portfolio has at least 7 images including project screenshots. Loading all images immediately increases time to interactive and causes visible layout shifts.
Fix — Add loading="lazy" to all images except the hero:
<!-- Hero image — no lazy loading (above fold) -->
Important: Add explicit width and height attributes to every img tag to prevent Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

9. TARGET STATE — WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
When all recommendations in this document have been implemented, the portfolio should produce this experience for a technical recruiter:
Page loads in under 2 seconds. Clean, dark, confident.
Hero: One sentence. One clear identity. Four engineering-specific stats.
Two CTAs. A professional photo. Nothing else.
Projects (separate page): Three projects. Each one a real technical case study.
Architecture diagram. Model accuracy metric. Engineering decision rationale.
Live demo link. GitHub link. No broken links. No raw IPs.
Experience (separate page): Four roles in a clean visual timeline.
AI internship at the top. Rise for Impact below it.
Verdict: "This person builds real systems and ships them.
I know exactly who they are and what they do.
I want to talk to them."
Prepared for development handoff to GitHub Copilot or equivalent AI coding assistant
